fatal_errors: The hypothesis addresses HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile and fracture testing, whereas the target concerns composition screening in the Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W system followed by room-temperature compression of as-cast Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5.

It replaces the target intervention—rule-of-mixtures modulus validation, VEC/density calculations, and screening of 38,326 compositions—with an unsubstantiated imaging-augmented physics-informed neural network.
The claimed 20% accuracy improvement and 10-fold speedup have no cited evidence, derivation, specified error metric, or defensible computational baseline.
No supporting prior evidence is identified.
Microstructural descriptors acquired during the same tensile or fracture test used to determine the target properties risk outcome leakage and may not enable prospective pre-test prediction.
explanation: There is only broad alignment with the desire to predict mechanical properties more efficiently. The proposed material, intervention, loading mode, mechanism, baseline, and outcomes do not reconstruct the target study. The target used a simple composition-based modulus/VEC/density screen to select a low-VEC refractory HEA, then demonstrated greatly enhanced compressive ductility while retaining high strength; it did not predict fracture toughness with a neural network. The generated mechanism is generically plausible but unsupported and omits the target's proposed VEC–Peierls-barrier–dislocation-mobility relationship. Its boundary conditions mention sensible imaging and domain-shift limitations, but fail to recognize key exclusions such as processing history, grain size, phase constitution, and defects. The blinded comparison is directionally testable, yet lacks an independent locked training set, explicit test-set size, fixed metrics, uncertainty handling, and a fair timing protocol; moreover, using in-test images can leak information about the measured response. Thus it is a speculative alternative rather than an evidence-supported reconstruction.
